Private equity secondaries have become one of the fastest-growing corners of finance, on track for a record year.

The market closed the first half of 2026 at a record $121bn and is tracking toward $250-260bn for the year, roughly double 2022.

GP-led continuation funds are the engine, letting managers hold prized companies longer while giving early investors an exit.

There is a quiet giant growing inside private markets, and most people outside finance have never heard of it. Private equity secondaries, the business of buying and selling existing stakes in private funds, has exploded from a niche corner into one of the most important sources of liquidity on Wall Street. When companies stay private for longer and traditional exits slow down, this is the pressure valve that lets money keep moving. Right now that valve is wide open.

The numbers are striking. The secondaries market closed the first half of 2026 at a record 121 billion dollars in volume, and the full year is tracking toward 250 to 270 billion, well over double what changed hands in 2022. That follows a record 240 billion dollar year in 2025, itself up almost half on the year before. In an era when initial public offerings and buyout exits have been patchy, private equity secondaries have quietly become the release valve the whole system leans on.

Secondaries have become the liquidity engine of private markets as companies stay private for longer. Photo by Anne Nygård on Unsplash

What private equity secondaries actually are

Strip away the jargon and the idea is simple. When an investor puts money into a private equity fund, that capital is normally locked up for a decade. A secondary transaction lets that investor sell the stake early to someone else, freeing up cash before the fund winds down. On the other side, buyers get access to mature portfolios with a clearer view of what they are buying. It is a second-hand market for private assets, and like any good marketplace, it thrives when both sellers and buyers have reasons to trade.

Two forces have supercharged it. First, a long stretch of slow exits left investors starved for cash, so many chose to sell stakes rather than wait. Second, and more importantly, fund managers themselves have embraced the tool. The fastest-growing slice of private equity secondaries is the GP-led deal, where a manager moves a prized company out of an ageing fund and into a new vehicle it also controls, giving existing investors the option to cash out or roll over.

The continuation-fund surge

These continuation funds have gone from a curiosity to a cornerstone. GP-led secondaries hit around 65 billion dollars in the first half of 2026, up about 35 per cent year on year, after reaching 115 billion for all of 2025. The biggest managers have raised war chests to match the demand. Here is the scale of the flagship funds now hunting for deals.

Why it matters beyond Wall Street

A healthy secondaries market is not just plumbing for financiers. It sets prices for private assets that would otherwise be hard to value, and it gives pensions, endowments and family offices a way to rebalance without waiting a decade. As more capital shifts from public markets into private ones, the ability to trade those private stakes becomes ever more important. In that sense, private equity secondaries are quietly underpinning the whole shift toward private capital that has reshaped finance over the past decade.

2026 should mark a record year for exits and secondaries volume, with buyers able to offer higher prices as cashflows move forward.

The questions worth asking

Growth this fast invites scrutiny, and it should. GP-led deals raise a genuine conflict: a manager is effectively selling a company from one of its funds to another of its funds, setting the price on both sides. Done well, with independent valuation and a fair option for investors to exit, it is a useful tool. Done carelessly, it can look like a way to avoid an honest reckoning on a struggling asset. Buyers also have to price patiently, because a stake bought too dear in a hot market can disappoint. None of this is investment advice, but it is why the smartest players treat discipline as the whole game.

For now, the momentum is unmistakable, and the biggest names in finance are betting it lasts. For more, read our features on how hedge funds took over the boardroom, the rise of the modern family office, the latest Fed rate decision, and our wider Finance coverage.

Who is buying, and why it is broadening

For years, secondaries were the preserve of a handful of specialist funds. That is changing fast. Pension funds, insurers and sovereign investors have piled in as buyers, drawn by the chance to put money to work in mature portfolios with a clearer view of value and, often, at a discount to what the assets are formally worth. Just as importantly, the market is reaching individual investors for the first time, through evergreen and semi-liquid vehicles that give wealthier savers a route into private equity secondaries without locking their money away for a decade. That democratisation is bringing a wave of fresh capital.

Pricing tells you how healthy the market is. In tougher years, stakes changed hands at steep discounts to their net asset value, as sellers accepted less to get liquidity. As confidence has returned and exits have picked up, those discounts have narrowed and buyers have been willing to pay closer to full value, a clear sign of demand outrunning supply. The split between LP-led deals, where an investor simply sells a stake, and GP-led deals, where a manager restructures a fund, has settled into a rough balance, with continuation vehicles now accounting for around half of all volume. It is a market that has grown up quickly and, so far, kept its footing.

The bigger picture is a structural shift, not a passing fad. As companies stay private for longer and public listings remain patchy, the plumbing that lets private ownership change hands has had to grow up, and private equity secondaries are that plumbing. Regulators are paying closer attention as the market scales and touches ordinary savers, which is healthy: transparency around valuations and fees is exactly what a maturing market needs. If the big managers keep that discipline, secondaries could become as routine a part of finance as the bond market, a permanent release valve rather than a crisis-era workaround.

From an obscure back-office trade to a market measured in hundreds of billions, private equity secondaries have arrived. Whether they can keep this pace as exits reopen is the question every allocator is now weighing.
